prompt.context: Transantiago is the public transportation system of Santiago de Chile. It is managed by the Ministry of Transportation and has more than 5 million users, integrating all the city's urban buses and subway. Transantiago's main source of revenue is the one generated by the tickets sold. They have two types of tickets: one normal ticket at a price of 2 dollars per trip, and one discounted ticket at a price of 1 dollar. With this revenue, plus a fixed subsidy of 900 Million USD, Transantiago must cover all their operating costs of the year. It is April 2021.
prompt.question: The Ministry of Transportation has called you because, after Covid-19, Transantiago has been experiencing a substantial decrease in demand and is worried if they will be able to cover all their operating costs. They want you to investigate all the possible impacts of Covid-19 and see how Transantiago will be able to cover all their operating costs this year.

clarifying_info.q: What is the main goal of this engagement?
clarifying_info.a: The main goal is to see if Transantiago will be able to cover all their operating costs this year.

clarifying_info.q: Are there other sources of revenue beyond tickets?
clarifying_info.a: The only actual source of revenue is the transportation tickets sold (plus the fixed subsidy of 900M USD).

clarifying_info.q: Can a single ticket be used on both buses and the subway?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, each ticket can be used in buses and subway or mixing both.

clarifying_info.q: What determines the ticket price — normal vs. discounted?
clarifying_info.a: The only price discrimination is whether the passenger is a student or not. Students pay the discounted price of 1 USD.

exhibits.title: Demand Forecast
exhibits.shows: A table of total trips projected for 2021, split by ticket type (Normal Ticket and Students), with three Covid-19 impact scenarios (Optimist, Neutral, Pessimist) each assigned a probability, and the expected price per ticket type.

exhibits.title: Initial Costs Projection
exhibits.shows: A breakdown of total projected operating costs (2,000 MM USD) split between Buses (1,500 MM) and Subway (500 MM), with sub-line items including maintenance, fuel/electricity (with volume and unit-price detail), drivers, and other costs, plus a list of Covid-19 effects on specific cost lines.

data.Bus Fuel: 500 MM USD (1,000 MM km x 0.5 Lt/km x 1 USD/lt)
data.Subway Electricity: 100 MM USD (200 MM km x 1 Kwh/km x 0.5 USD/Kwh)
data.Covid-19 effects: Oil price -20% vs. projected; Electricity price -10% vs. projected; Night curfews (buses only): bus driver cost -10%, total bus kilometres -10%

framework: Revenue: Ticket Revenue (Normal + Student) + Fixed Subsidy
Ticket Revenue: Number of Trips x Price per Ticket (impacted by Covid-19 demand scenarios)
Operating Costs: Buses (maintenance, fuel, drivers, other) + Subway (maintenance, electricity, drivers, other)
Covid-19 impacts on both revenue side (demand drop) and cost side (oil/electricity prices, curfew-driven reductions)
Risks and Limitations: uncertainty in scenario realisation, forecast variability, social/public-service consequences of each action
Possible solutions to close any identified gap

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, calculate the expected total revenue from ticket sales in 2021 after Covid-19 demand impacts.
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute a probability-weighted expected Covid impact for each ticket type, apply it to projected trips to get expected demand, then multiply by the respective price. A strong candidate notes that the pessimistic scenario carries significant downside risk and that relying on expected values alone understates that risk.

math.setup: Expected Impact = sum(probability x scenario impact) for each ticket type. Expected Demand = Projected Demand x (1 + Expected Impact). Revenue = Price x Expected Demand.
steps: Normal Ticket expected Covid impact = 0.3x(-10%) + 0.4x(-20%) + 0.3x(-30%) = -3% - 8% - 9% = -20%
Normal Ticket expected demand = 500 MM x (1 - 20%) = 400 MM trips
Normal Ticket revenue = 2 USD x 400 MM = 800 MM USD
Student expected demand = 100 MM x (1 - 63%) = 37 MM trips
Student revenue = 1 USD x 37 MM = 37 MM USD
Total ticket revenue = 800 MM + 37 MM = 837 MM USD
Total revenue = 837 MM (tickets) + 900 MM (subsidy) = 1,737 MM USD
math.answer: Total ticket revenue = 837 MM USD; Total revenue including subsidy = 1,737 MM USD

questions.prompt: Before seeing Exhibit 2, brainstorm the main operating cost categories for a public transportation system like Transantiago and how Covid-19 might affect each.
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify most of the cost lines that appear in Exhibit 2: fuel/electricity, vehicle maintenance, driver salaries, and other overhead for both buses and subway. Covid-19 effects to mention: reduced ridership lowering variable costs, curfews reducing service hours and driver requirements, energy price changes, potential increased cleaning/sanitation costs.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, calculate the new total expected operating costs after Covid-19 effects.
questions.guidance: Candidate must identify the three cost lines that change (fuel, electricity, bus drivers), compute each new value using the given unit-price and volume adjustments, calculate the savings versus the original projection, and subtract savings from the original 2,000 MM total. Candidate should handle unit conversions (MM km x Lt/km x USD/Lt) correctly.

math.setup: Three changes: (1) Bus fuel cost changes due to -10% km and -20% oil price. (2) Subway electricity cost changes due to -10% electricity price. (3) Bus drivers cost changes due to -10% curfew reduction.
steps: New Total Bus km = 1,000 MM x (1 - 10%) = 900 MM km
New Oil Price = 1 USD/lt x (1 - 20%) = 0.8 USD/lt
New Fuel Cost = 900 MM km x 0.5 Lt/km x 0.8 USD/lt = 360 MM USD
Change in Fuel Cost = 500 MM - 360 MM = 140 MM USD saved
New Electricity Price = 0.5 USD/Kwh x (1 - 10%) = 0.45 USD/Kwh
New Electricity Cost = 200 MM km x 1 Kwh/km x 0.45 USD/Kwh = 90 MM USD
Change in Electricity Cost = 100 MM - 90 MM = 10 MM USD saved
New Bus Drivers Cost = 500 MM x (1 - 10%) = 450 MM USD
Change in Bus Drivers Cost = 500 MM - 450 MM = 50 MM USD saved
Total savings = 140 MM + 10 MM + 50 MM = 200 MM USD
New Total Costs = 2,000 MM - 200 MM = 1,800 MM USD
math.answer: New total operating costs = 1,800 MM USD

questions.prompt: Combine your revenue and cost analysis: will Transantiago be able to cover its operating costs? What is the gap?
questions.guidance: Candidate links the two calculations. Revenue (tickets + subsidy) = 1,737 MM USD. Costs = 1,800 MM USD. Gap = -63 MM USD deficit. Strong candidate flags that this is based on expected/average scenario values and that the pessimistic scenario would produce a much larger deficit; the numbers carry significant forecast uncertainty.

steps: Total Revenue = 837 MM (tickets) + 900 MM (subsidy) = 1,737 MM USD
Total Costs = 1,800 MM USD
Profit = 1,737 MM - 1,800 MM = -63 MM USD

brainstorming.prompt: Transantiago faces a 63 MM USD deficit. What solutions would you consider to close this gap?

categories.name: Revenue — pricing
ideas: Increase the normal ticket price (e.g., raise by ~13 cents / ~6% to generate ~63 MM additional revenue assuming demand holds)
Add premium express or limited-stop routes at a higher fare

categories.name: Revenue — demand stimulation
ideas: Invest in safety and hygiene measures to rebuild passenger confidence and increase ridership (requires ~31.5 MM additional normal-ticket trips to close the gap)
Marketing campaign to encourage return to public transit
Improve frequency and reliability to attract back riders

categories.name: Revenue — other sources
ideas: Seek additional government subsidy (+63 MM USD = ~7% increase)
Partnerships and advertising revenue on buses/stations
Commercial concessions (retail kiosks, vending) in stations

categories.name: Cost reduction
ideas: Reduce total bus kilometres operated to cut fuel and driver costs (a ~17% further reduction in bus km, i.e., ~160 MM km, would close the gap)
Negotiate lower fuel and electricity contracts
Defer non-critical maintenance to a future period
Optimise driver scheduling to reduce overtime and part-time costs

categories.name: Other / wait-and-see
ideas: Wait until July 2021 to observe which demand scenario is materialising before taking costly or irreversible actions
Build a contingency reserve request into the budget in case pessimistic scenario occurs
Explore short-term borrowing or budget reallocation within the Ministry

recommendation: After analysis, Transantiago faces an expected deficit of 63 MM USD in 2021 under the average scenario. We recommend a two-part approach: (1) immediately request a targeted additional subsidy of 63 MM USD from the government — a 7% increase — as the fastest and least socially disruptive lever; and (2) initiate a demand-recovery plan (enhanced safety protocols, marketing) to rebuild ridership and reduce structural dependence on subsidies beyond 2021.

Alternatively, if additional subsidy is not available, a modest normal-ticket price increase of approximately 13 cents (6%) combined with a targeted reduction in low-demand bus routes could close the gap with limited impact on core service levels.
risks: All figures are based on probability-weighted scenario averages; the pessimistic scenario (30% probability) would produce a significantly larger deficit than 63 MM USD
Student ticket prices cannot be changed in 2021, limiting pricing flexibility
Reducing kilometres or raising prices may suppress ridership further, creating a negative demand spiral
Social and political sensitivity of cutting public transport services or raising fares during a pandemic
Forecast uncertainty across all cost and demand inputs — actual results could deviate materially in either direction
next_steps: Monitor actual demand weekly through April–June to determine which scenario is materialising and trigger contingency actions if trajectory is pessimistic
Engage Ministry of Finance immediately regarding additional subsidy request with supporting analysis
Commission a route-level efficiency analysis to identify specific low-utilisation routes that could be reduced with minimal social impact
Review fuel and electricity procurement contracts for 2022 to lock in lower prices
